summary:
AQUA PULSE is an interactive web application that explores the hidden history of Monterrey’s water crisis. It brings together satellite imagery, reservoir records, weather data, and urban growth maps to help people understand changes in three essential reservoirs: Cerro Prieto, La Boca, and El Cuchillo.

We developed a map-based dashboard that uses Sentinel-1 radar observations to estimate changes in surface-water extent, Sentinel-2 imagery for visual context, and NASA NISAR imagery and catalog metadata to explore recent radar observations. Users can compare satellite evidence with official reservoir storage records, rainfall, and the expansion of built-up areas.

The project addresses the challenge by making complex radar data accessible through a local story with clear social relevance. It distinguishes water surface area from stored volume and makes data gaps and uncertainty visible.

Water shortages affect daily life, public health, and economic activity. AQUA PULSE helps communities explore the evidence behind those shortages and supports more informed conversations about water resilience.
details:
AQUA PULSE turns satellite observations and public records into an interactive exploration of Monterrey’s water crisis. It focuses on three reservoirs that supply the region: Cerro Prieto, La Boca, and El Cuchillo.

How it works

Users explore a map and timeline to compare reservoir conditions, weather, and urban growth. The application combines:

  • Sentinel-1 radar observations to estimate candidate surface-water extent, including during cloudy conditions.
  • Sentinel-2 optical imagery to provide visual context.
  • NASA NISAR catalog metadata and official browse imagery to explore recent radar observations, their dates, coverage, and product maturity.
  • Official reservoir records from CONAGUA, SADM, and the Government of Nuevo León to show reported water storage.
  • ERA5 weather data and GHSL built-up surface estimates to explore environmental conditions and the region’s expansion.

The dashboard also includes exploratory storage scenarios based on historical changes. These scenarios help users examine possible trajectories while keeping their assumptions visible.

Benefits and intended impact

AQUA PULSE makes technical Earth-observation data easier to understand through a familiar local issue. Residents, students, journalists, and decision-makers can compare evidence from multiple sources in one place.

Our intended impact is to strengthen water literacy and support informed conversations about drought, infrastructure, and regional resilience. The application helps users investigate relationships between water, weather, and urban development without presenting those relationships as proof of causation.

Tools and development

We built the application with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Leaflet for interactive maps and Node.js for the server, catalog queries, and build process. Python supported geospatial processing through NumPy, Rasterio, Shapely, SciPy, scikit-image, Pillow, Requests, and pyproj. NASA CMR supplies searchable NISAR metadata, and NASA GIBS supplies imagery. The project runs on a standard computer through a web browser.

What makes it creative

The project connects observations from space with the lived experience of a city facing water insecurity. Its map and timeline bring reservoir changes, official storage measurements, weather, and urban expansion into a shared visual story. It also connects historical Sentinel observations with recent NISAR imagery, showing how different missions contribute complementary evidence.

Factors we considered

Scientific clarity guided the design. Water surface area and stored volume are different measurements, so we display them separately. We preserve acquisition dates, source attribution, product maturity, and missing observations. NISAR browse images provide visual evidence; numerical analysis of NISAR scientific pixels remains future work.

We also considered accessibility, mobile use, limited connectivity, and reproducibility. Locally stored imagery and records support exploration when live services are unavailable, while source links and documented methods help others examine how the results were produced.
